newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees sensitive trade surplus $9 bln in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China sees sensitive trade surplus $9 bln in 1997.

text.p: Chinese statisticians expect the nation's diplomatically-sensitive trade balance to total $9.0 billion in 1997, the official China Securities newspaper said on Friday.

Exports would increase by around nine percent from 1996, while imports would grow by about 10 percent, the newspaper said in a report issued just a day after the official Xinhua news agency predicted the 1997 surplus would be around $20 billion.
China's trade performance has become an increasingly sensitive issue in its fragile ties with Washington, long strained by Beijing's growing cross-Pacific trade surplus.
The new lower figure, which China Securities sourced to the State Statistical Bureau, could well be an attempt by Beijing to downplay expectations, said a Hong Kong-based China economist.
"The trade balance (has) become increasingly politicised because of China's relationship with the U.S.," the economist, who declined to be identified, said by telephone.
Washington says its trade deficit with China climbed to nearly $29 billion in the first nine months of the year from $25 billion in the same period last year.
The trade deficit, the second largest for the U.S. after its gap with Japan, was seen reaching $40 billion by the end of the year, up from $34 billion in 1995.
Beijing could try to play down estimates of future trade to give itself diplomatic ammunition in its bid to enter the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the economist said.
"It (politics) does affect overall announcements on trade because they're very conscious now of wanting to get into WTO," he said.
Beijing has been seeking to join the global trade body on favourable terms as a developing nation, but Washington has insisted that China's economy is too big for such treatment.

A group of influential U.S. senators recently petitioned President Bill Clinton to reject China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation on special terms because it would harm American economic interests.
China's trade surplus would likely be between $13 billion to $14 billion next year, the economist said, adding that Beijing would be cautious with its trade predicitions.
"It doesn't necessarily help to come out with a low number, but it hurts to come out with a high number," he said.
